name: Tsotsitaal
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.citation: one of the works listed for this language (see the second reader's note)
new_statements.check: reported by the second reader, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work was listed for tsot1242 and it was opened, so there were no listed silent/unopened works to spot-check; instead I spot-checked the earlier-pass files that records as silent, by a full-text search for stress/accent each saved text for stress/penult/prosod/tone/tonal/pitch/intonation/klemtoon/aksent. Ditsele & Hurst 2016, Bembe 2008, Mojela 2003, Gumede 2017, Olivier 2015: no phonological hits (Olivier's hits are 'beklemtoon' = 'emphasises'; Gumede's are 'stress' = psychological stress in ethics forms). Hurst 2008 pp. ~180 (the text layer): 'pitch' and 'tone' appear only as lay descriptors of a shouting/urban speaking style, not phonology. Aycard 2014 p. 108 (the text layer): de…

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2013. Change Request 2013-017 [fly] (submitted by Ellen Hurst, UCT).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Administrative: renames [fly] from Tsotsitaal to Flaaitaal (the Afrikaans-based variety), keeping Tsotsitaal as alternate name; cites Mesthrie & Hurst 2013. Nothing linguistic.

sources.citation: Gumede, Zempilo S. 2017. A linguistic analysis of the isiZulu variety of tsotsitaal in the Mandeni district in KwaZulu-Natal. MTech thesis, Tshwane University of Technology.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 2.2.3 'Phonology' (p. 20) gives only a definition and a vowel-coalescence example (na+umagriza > nomagriza) and states 'This study is not going to deal with phonology in detail'; nothing on stress. Zulu-based variety, not Flaaitaal.

sources.citation: Ditsele, Thabo & Ellen Hurst. 2016. Travelling terms and local innovations: the tsotsitaal of the North West province, South Africa. Literator 37(2): a1274.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lexical study; nothing on stress or phonology.

sources.citation: Olivier, Jako. 2015. Afrikaanse transtaling en taaloorgang: die napraat van Tsotsitaal en Swartafrikaans. Stilet 27(2): 63-82.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Discusses non-standard vowel/diphthong pronunciations in two poems; no statement on word stress (klem/aksent).

sources.citation: Aycard, Pierre. 2014. The use of Iscamtho by children in White City-Jabavu, Soweto: slang and language contact in an African urban context. PhD thesis, University of Cape Town. 441 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement for Tsotsitaal/Flaaitaal. One incidental remark on the Zulu-based Iscamtho of Soweto: the borrowed question word 'wayi' shows 'a lengthening of the first syllable of the word, according to Zulu prosody, which requires the penultimate syllable to be long' (ch. 6, Excerpt 1 discussion, p. ~151). Also summarises the literature (Schuring 1983/1985, Msimang 1987, Makhudu 1995/2002, Gunnink 2012).

sources.citation: Bembe, Magdeline P. 2008. The use of slang among black youth in Gauteng. MA, University of Johannesburg (40-page file).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or phonology.

sources.citation: Hurst, Ellen. 2008. Style, structure and function in Cape Town Tsotsitaal. PhD thesis, University of Cape Town. 231 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on word stress; sociolinguistic/MLF study of the Xhosa-based Cape Town variety; only remarks on 'accent'/'tone' as lay speaker perceptions of city style (pp. around lines 8335-8704 of text).

sources.citation: Mojela, V.M. 2003. Review of Louis Molamu, Tsotsitaal: A dictionary of the language of Sophiatown. Lexikos 13: 334-337.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Reports that the dictionary has no phonetic transcriptions and inconsistent spelling so 'it is not always clear how some of the terms are pronounced' (p. 337); the review describes the front matter (sources of information, micro/macrostructure) and mentions no phonology or stress section.

sources.citation: Calteaux, Karen. 1996. Standard and non-standard African language varieties in the urban areas of South Africa. Main report for the STANON research programme. Pretoria: HSRC. (ERIC ED402752, 258 pp.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 3.4.5.6 describes Tsotsitaal/Iscamtho sociolinguistically (no phonology). Section 4.9 'Stress' (p. 100) is about the African languages generally: 'The African languages are characterised by the occurrence of stress (or rather length) on the penultimate syllable' (citing Thipa 1989 on Xhosa) and says stress patterns are not affected by language contact; it does not describe Tsotsitaal stress.

sources.citation: Gilbert, Glenn G. & Dennis Makhudu. 1987. Le continuum créole en « Afrikaans » : une perspective non-eurocentrique. Études créoles 10(2): 15-24.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Compares Standard Afrikaans, Coloured Afrikaans and Flytaal on Hancock's 50 sentences; may comment on prosody; open on Persée but the PDF is behind a bot challenge.

sources.citation: Makhudu, K.D.P. 2002. An introduction to Flaaitaal (or Tsotsitaal). In R. Mesthrie (ed.), Language in South Africa, 398-406. Cambridge: CUP. (Earlier version: Makhudu 1995, in Language and Social History, 298-305, Cape Town: David Philip.)
